claim: The segmentation clock is comprised of a population of coordinated oscillating cells that together produce rhythmic gene expression patterns in the embryo.
source: This clock is comprised of a population of coordinated oscillating cells that together produce rhythmic gene expression patterns in the embryo.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the composition of the segmentation clock, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Individual cells can behave as autonomous cellular oscillators.
source: We demonstrate that individual cells can behave as autonomous cellular oscillators.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from single cell recordings.

claim: Single cells have longer periods than the tissue.
source: Single cells have longer periods and lower precision than the tissue, highlighting the role of collective processes in the segmentation clock.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements comparing single cells to tissue-level oscillations.

claim: Single cells have lower precision than the tissue.
source: Single cells have longer periods and lower precision than the tissue, highlighting the role of collective processes in the segmentation clock.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements of quality factors.

claim: Persistent oscillating gene expression within the tailbud and PSM corresponds to segment formation in chick, mouse, and zebrafish.
source: Persistent oscillating gene expression within the tailbud and PSM corresponds to segment formation in chick, mouse, and zebrafish (Palmeirim et al., 1997; Dequéant et al., 2006; Krol et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Circadian clock neurons demonstrate autonomy by recording daily oscillations in firing rate and gene expression from single cells for several cycles in the absence of their neighbors.
source: The autonomy of circadian clock neurons was demonstrated by recording daily oscillations in firing rate and gene expression from single cells for several cycles in the absence of their neighbors (Welsh et al., 1995; Webb et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies on circadian clock neurons.

claim: Some microbial systems produce oscillations only when at critical densities that allowed cell-to-cell communication, otherwise the isolated cells were not rhythmic.
source: In contrast, some microbial systems have been shown to produce oscillations only when at critical densities that allowed cell-to-cell communication, otherwise the isolated cells were not rhythmic (Gregor et al., 2010; Danino et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies on microbial systems.

claim: Gene expression in explanted PSM can oscillate in the absence of neighboring tissues.
source: Historically, the term autonomy has appeared many times in the segmentation clock literature, starting with the observation that gene expression in explanted PSM can oscillate in the absence of neighboring tissues (Palmeirim et al., 1997; 1998; Maroto et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies on explanted PSM.

claim: The PSM is autonomous at the tissue level.
source: This means the PSM is autonomous at the tissue level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that explanted PSM can oscillate in the absence of neighboring tissues.

claim: An auto-regulatory negative feedback loop arising from the transcription and translation of members of the Hes/Her gene family would be consistent with a cell-autonomous mechanism.
source: The possibility for an auto-regulatory negative feedback loop arising from the transcription and translation of members of the Hes/Her gene family would be consistent with a cell-autonomous mechanism (Hirata et al., 2002; Lewis, 2003; Monk, 2003), and oscillations in this gene family have been observed across vertebrate species (Krol et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Oscillations in the Hes/Her gene family have been observed across vertebrate species.
source: The possibility for an auto-regulatory negative feedback loop arising from the transcription and translation of members of the Hes/Her gene family would be consistent with a cell-autonomous mechanism (Hirata et al., 2002; Lewis, 2003; Monk, 2003), and oscillations in this gene family have been observed across vertebrate species (Krol et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Oscillations in the Delta-Notch system have been discovered in all vertebrates.
source: However, the discovery of oscillations in the Delta-Notch system in all vertebrates and in many genes of the Wnt and FGF intercellular signaling pathways in mouse and chick, raises the possibility that communication between cells may play a critical role in the generation and/or maintenance of the oscillations (Dequéant et al., 2006; Krol et al., 2011; Goldbeter and Pourquié, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Oscillations in many genes of the Wnt and FGF intercellular signaling pathways have been discovered in mouse and chick.
source: However, the discovery of oscillations in the Delta-Notch system in all vertebrates and in many genes of the Wnt and FGF intercellular signaling pathways in mouse and chick, raises the possibility that communication between cells may play a critical role in the generation and/or maintenance of the oscillations (Dequéant et al., 2006; Krol et al., 2011; Goldbeter and Pourquié, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells isolated from chick PSM, then cultured in suspension and fixed at subsequent time intervals, showed changes in cyclic gene expression.
source: In the first study, cells isolated from chick PSM, then cultured in suspension and fixed at subsequent time intervals, showed changes in cyclic gene expression (Maroto et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The authors of the chick study were not able to distinguish between noisy autonomous oscillators and stochastic patterns of gene expression due to the unavoidable uncertainty in reconstructing a time series from static snapshots of different cells.
source: Due to the unavoidable uncertainty in reconstructing a time series from static snapshots of different cells, the authors of this study were not able to distinguish between noisy autonomous oscillators and stochastic patterns of gene expression, and highlighted the need for real-time reporters to investigate the autonomy of PSM cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the chick study and describes its limitations.

claim: Individual mouse PSM cells showed at most 4 expression pulses with variable duration and amplitude, which appeared to damp out.
source: Three cells were reported, showing at most 4 expression pulses with variable duration and amplitude, which appeared to damp out.
evidence: This statement describes findings from a previous study on mouse PSM cells.

claim: The mouse PSM cell study concluded that PSM cells may be "unstable" oscillators.
source: This study concluded that PSM cells may be "unstable" oscillators, and highlighted the role of intercellular coupling for maintenance of oscillations.
evidence: This statement describes the conclusion of a previous study.

claim: Treatment of zebrafish embryos with a γ-secretase inhibitor targeting the Notch intercellular domain (DAPT) leads to a loss of spatial coherence in oscillating gene expression.
source: Treatment of zebrafish embryos with a γ-secretase inhibitor targeting the Notch intercellular domain (DAPT) leads to a loss of spatial coherence in oscillating gene expression (Riedel-Kruse et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Imaging of individual cells in mutant embryos with reduced Notch signaling show that oscillations persist under these conditions.
source: Additionally, imaging of individual cells in mutant embryos with reduced Notch signaling show that oscillations persist under these conditions (Delaune et al., 2012), though this does not rule out the possibility of Notch or other signaling factors playing a role in promoting oscillations.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Explanted intact tailbuds from 8-somite stage embryos homozygous for the Looping transgene showed persistent Her1-YFP oscillations.
source: We observed persistent Her1-YFP oscillations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) that did not slow down (period 42.5 ± 11.4 min (mean ± SD) at 26°C) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from explanted tailbuds.

claim: Explanted tailbuds had a period of 42.5 ± 11.4 min (mean ± SD) at 26°C.
source: We observed persistent Her1-YFP oscillations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) that did not slow down (period 42.5 ± 11.4 min (mean ± SD) at 26°C) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Individual cells cultured in serum-only conditions displayed a few pulses that appeared to damp out early in the recording.
source: In identical culture conditions to the explanted tailbuds, most individual cells that expressed Her1-YFP displayed a few pulses that appeared to damp out early in the recording (N = 2 independent cultures, n = 52 total cells, median cycles = 2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from cell cultures.

claim: When Fgf8b was added to cell cultures, a persistent rhythmic behavior was observed.
source: In contrast to the serum-only treatment, when Fgf8b was added to part of the same cell suspension within a divided imaging dish, a persistent rhythmic behavior was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing serum-only to serum+Fgf8b conditions.

claim: The number of cycles increased dramatically when Fgf8b was added, spanning the recording interval and without altering the period.
source: The number of cycles increased dramatically, spanning the recording interval and without altering the period (N = 4 independent cultures, n = 547 total cells; median cycles = 5; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: More than 50% of cells in the in vitro population of Looping tailbud cells expressed the Her1-YFP reporter.
source: An imaged field contained 15 to 20 cells (Figure 1B, black arrowheads) and more than 50% of these cells (321/547) had YFP signal (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Cells from the same embryos cultured in parallel maintained tailbud marker expression.
source: Cells from the same embryos cultured in parallel maintained tailbud marker expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 6, Figure 1—figure supplement 7), suggesting that under these conditions the cells retain a tailbud progenitor phenotype (Martin and Kimelman, 2010; 2012).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from immunocytochemistry.

claim: From the 321 cells that were YFP-positive at the beginning of the recording, 189 autonomous cells remained after excluding cells that moved, died, or touched another cell.
source: From the 321 cells that were YFP-positive at the beginning of the recording, we first excluded from analysis any cell that moved out of the imaging field, died, or touched another cell either through movement or division at any point in the recording. From the remaining 189 autonomous cells, we observed rhythmic expression (two or more pulses of expression) in 147, which we term the low-density data set (Figure 1B–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 5; Figure 1—source data 2; Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This describes the data analysis process and the resulting dataset.

claim: 147 autonomous cells showed rhythmic expression (two or more pulses of expression), termed the low-density data set.
source: From the remaining 189 autonomous cells, we observed rhythmic expression (two or more pulses of expression) in 147, which we term the low-density data set (Figure 1B–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 5; Figure 1—source data 2; Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This describes the primary dataset used for analysis.

claim: A distribution of periods (78.8 ± 15.3 min [mean ± SD from 442 cycles]) was found in the low-density data set.
source: We found a distribution of periods (78.8 ± 15.3 min [mean ± SD from 442 cycles]) and amplitudes (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements.

claim: No systematic slowing in successive oscillations was observed in the data, suggesting that the cultures were stationary over this interval.
source: Importantly, we observed no systematic slowing in successive oscillations in our data suggesting that the cultures were stationary over this interval (Figure 1—figure supplement 8E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: The Her1-YFP signal co-localized with the nuclear mCherry signal, which did not oscillate.
source: We found that the Her1-YFP signal co-localized with the nuclear mCherry signal, which did not oscillate (n = 8 cells, Figure 1E, EI) indicating that focal drift does not contribute strongly to changes in YFP intensity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from dual-labeled cells.

claim: Focal drift does not contribute strongly to changes in YFP intensity.
source: We found that the Her1-YFP signal co-localized with the nuclear mCherry signal, which did not oscillate (n = 8 cells, Figure 1E, EI) indicating that focal drift does not contribute strongly to changes in YFP intensity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the nuclear mCherry signal did not oscillate.

claim: Cells from the zebrafish tailbud do not need cell-cell contact to maintain oscillations.
source: Combined, these results show that cells from the zebrafish tailbud do not need cell-cell contact to maintain oscillations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing oscillations in isolated cells.

claim: Fully isolated cells can sustain oscillations.
source: We found that these fully isolated cells can also sustain oscillations (N = 5, n = 10, period = 62 ± 21 min (mean ± SD), median cycles = 5) (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 9; Figure 1—source data 1; Video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from single cells in 96-well plates.

claim: Fully isolated cells had a period of 62 ± 21 min (mean ± SD) and median cycles of 5.
source: We found that these fully isolated cells can also sustain oscillations (N = 5, n = 10, period = 62 ± 21 min (mean ± SD), median cycles = 5) (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 9; Figure 1—source data 1; Video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements.

claim: A population of autonomously oscillating cells from the zebrafish segmentation clock exists.
source: Together, these data reveal the existence of a population of autonomously oscillating cells from the zebrafish segmentation clock.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing oscillations in isolated cells.

claim: Mechanisms of oscillation in zebrafish based on reaction-diffusion processes, which rely on diffusion across the tissue and do not contain cell-autonomous oscillators, are not supported by the results.
source: Mechanisms of oscillation in zebrafish based on reaction-diffusion processes (Meinhardt and Gierer, 2000), and which rely on diffusion across the tissue and do not contain cell-autonomous oscillators, are therefore not supported by our results.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing cell-autonomous oscillations.

claim: In nearly all cases the period of individual cells is longer than that of the tissue, indicating a role for tissue-level processes in setting the period of segmentation.
source: In addition, in nearly all cases the period of individual cells is longer than that of the tissue, indicating a role for tissue-level processes in setting the period of segmentation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the periods of individual cells to tissue-level oscillations.

claim: A remarkable feature of the oscillatory signals is their variability between cells in the population.
source: A remarkable feature of these oscillatory signals is their variability between cells in the population (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: A spectrum of behaviors is observed in the low-density data set including cells that start or stop oscillating during the experiment, cells that start and then stop, and stuttering rhythms where cycles are missed.
source: We observe a spectrum of behaviors in the low-density data set including cells that start or stop oscillating during the experiment, cells that start and then stop, and stuttering rhythms where cycles are missed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Amplitude displays a slow variation revealed by correlations.
source: Plotting amplitude and period of consecutive cycles from the whole low-density data set indicate that amplitude displays a slow variation revealed by correlations (Figure 2B), while period does not show any appreciable correlation at this timescale (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data analysis.

claim: Period does not show any appreciable correlation at this timescale.
source: Plotting amplitude and period of consecutive cycles from the whole low-density data set indicate that amplitude displays a slow variation revealed by correlations (Figure 2B), while period does not show any appreciable correlation at this timescale (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data analysis.

claim: No correlation was found between the period and amplitude of each cycle.
source: We did not find a correlation between the period and amplitude of each cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data analysis.

claim: Slow fluctuations in the parameter μ that controls the amplitude of oscillators can drive the oscillators in and out of the oscillatory state.
source: Slow fluctuations in the parameter μ that controls the amplitude of oscillators in the theory. Motivated by the lack of correlation between period and amplitude in the data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–I), we set the coupling between these processes to zero. Slow amplitude fluctuations can drive the oscillators in and out of the oscillatory state (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and introduce correlations in the amplitude of consecutive cycles that are comparable to the experimental data (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from theoretical modeling supported by simulations.

claim: Slow amplitude fluctuations introduce correlations in the amplitude of consecutive cycles that are comparable to the experimental data.
source: Slow amplitude fluctuations can drive the oscillators in and out of the oscillatory state (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and introduce correlations in the amplitude of consecutive cycles that are comparable to the experimental data (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from theoretical modeling supported by simulations.

claim: Additive white noise in the variables of the oscillator describes period fluctuations and their weak correlation observed in the data.
source: To describe period fluctuations and their weak correlation observed in the data we introduced an additive white noise in the variables of the oscillator (Figure 2C,G) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from theoretical modeling supported by simulations.

claim: A region in parameter space corresponds to the behavior of isolated cells in terms of the fraction of the total time that a cell oscillates.
source: We performed simulations over a range of values of correlation time and variance in μ and found a region in parameter space that corresponds to the behavior of isolated cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a finding from theoretical modeling supported by simulations.

claim: Changing the variance of the additive white noise did not affect the distribution of amplitudes, the correlations of amplitudes, or the fraction of the oscillating time.
source: In contrast to these effects, changing the variance of the additive white noise did not affect the distribution of amplitudes, the correlations of amplitudes, or the fraction of the oscillating time (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from theoretical modeling supported by simulations.

claim: The theory is consistent with a population of cells having the same oscillatory mechanism, captured during different time windows of their dynamics.
source: While these results cannot rule out potential cell-type differences in the population, the theory is consistent with a population of cells having the same oscillatory mechanism, captured during different time windows of their dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical modeling.

claim: The theory provides for the first time an observation of the longer timescales of noise in the autonomous oscillations of cells from the segmentation clock.
source: Importantly, it provides for the first time an observation of the longer timescales of noise in the autonomous oscillations of cells from the segmentation clock, regardless of its source.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical modeling and experimental data.

claim: From the 147 cells in the low-density data set, 54 cells exhibited persistent oscillatory behavior, defined as cells exhibiting sequential peaks over 80% of the recording time.
source: From the 147 cells in the low-density data set, we selected those cells with persistent oscillatory behavior, defined as cells exhibiting sequential peaks over 80% of the recording time (n = 54 cells; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the selection criteria for a subset of the data.

claim: Persistent cells had a mean period of 78.3 min.
source: We found that persistent cells had a mean period of 78.3 min (Figure 3B, inset).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements.

claim: A median quality factor QP ~4 was calculated from the persistent cells' oscillations.
source: We calculated a median quality factor QP ~4 from the persistent cells' oscillations (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The precision of dividing cells would be lower than that of persistent cells.
source: Our analysis excluded dividing cells, and as cell division is thought to introduce phase noise in the time series (Delaune et al., 2012), the precision of dividing cells would be lower.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous work showing that cell division introduces phase noise.

claim: A median quality factor QE ~10 was calculated in the embryo.
source: We calculated a median quality factor QE ~10 in the embryo (Figure 3B,C; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements from embryo data.

claim: The precision of the tissue level oscillations in vivo is a factor of 3 times higher than the typical persistent segmentation clock cell in vitro.
source: This value indicates that the precision of the tissue level oscillations in vivo is a factor of 3 times higher than the typical persistent segmentation clock cell in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the quality factors of cells and tissue.

claim: Coupling may increase the precision of the individual cells by a similar amount in the embryo.
source: This suggests that in the embryo, coupling may increase the precision of the individual cells by a similar amount.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of precision between cells and tissue.

claim: This increase in precision should be considered as a lower bound.
source: Given that there are many cells with lower Q factor than the median, including those that were too noisy to be included in the persistent oscillator set, this increase in precision should be considered as a lower bound.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the distribution of quality factors in the data.

claim: Single mammalian fibroblasts expressing a Period2-Luciferase reporter oscillated with a median quality factor QF ~20.
source: To place the precision of persistent cells in context with another autonomous cellular oscillator, we analyzed the precision of the circadian clock using time series from single mammalian fibroblasts expressing a Period2-Luciferase reporter (Leise et al., 2012) and found these cells oscillated with a median quality factor QF ~20 (Figure 3D; Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of circadian clock data.

claim: Cells isolated from the zebrafish segmentation clock are less precise than the mouse circadian clock in single cells.
source: Thus, cells isolated from the zebrafish segmentation clock are less precise than the mouse circadian clock in single cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the quality factors of segmentation clock cells and circadian clock cells.

claim: Noise in the parameter μ, which controls the amplitude, did not result in the observed range of quality factors.
source: We investigated the precision of simulated oscillators, comparing it to the experimental data. Noise in the parameter μ, which controls the amplitude and produced the heterogeneity of oscillator behavior discussed above, did not result in the observed range of quality factors (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from theoretical modeling supported by simulations.

claim: Introducing white noise in the variables of the SL oscillator described the precision of the data.
source: In contrast, introducing white noise in the variables of the SL oscillator described the precision of the data (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from theoretical modeling supported by simulations.

claim: The experimentally observed precision of persistent cells from the segmentation clock was located within a restricted range of variance in white noise.
source: The experimentally observed precision of persistent cells from the segmentation clock was located within a restricted range of variance in this noise (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from theoretical modeling supported by simulations.

claim: Single cell oscillators isolated from the zebrafish segmentation clock are autonomous.
source: Our findings improve understanding of the segmentation clock at both single cell and tissue level. Single cell oscillators isolated from the zebrafish segmentation clock are autonomous.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Tissue-level contributions aid in establishing the period and increasing the precision of segmentation.
source: Nevertheless, tissue-level contributions aid in establishing the period and increasing the precision of segmentation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Inhibiting the Delta-Notch pathway that mediates synchronization between neighboring oscillators results in slower segmentation in zebrafish.
source: In zebrafish, inhibiting the Delta-Notch pathway that mediates synchronization between neighboring oscillators results in slower segmentation (Herrgen et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The change in period from inhibiting Delta-Notch has been interpreted as the result of losing the collective effects of coupling with delays.
source: This change in period has been interpreted as the result of losing the collective effects of coupling with delays (Herrgen et al., 2010; Morelli et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An untested prediction is that an individual isolated tailbud cell should slow when removed from coupling within the tissue.
source: An untested prediction of this scenario is that an individual isolated tailbud cell should slow when removed from coupling within the tissue.
evidence: This is a prediction based on previous theoretical work.

claim: The period of the oscillations measured in tailbud explants (42.5 ± 11.4 min, mean ± SD) was longer than the segmentation period in intact embryos of 27 ± 1 min (± SD) at 26°C, a slowing of approximately 1.5-fold over the intact embryo.
source: We first noted that the period of the oscillations measured in tailbud explants (42.5 ± 11.4 min, mean ± SD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) was longer than the segmentation period in intact embryos of 27 ± 1 min (± SD) at 26°C (Schröter et al., 2008), a slowing of approximately 1.5-fold over the intact embryo.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental measurements from explants and intact embryos.

claim: A comparable increase in period was not reported with explanted mouse tailbuds.
source: A comparable increase in period was not reported with explanted mouse tailbuds (Masamizu et al., 2006; Lauschke et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies on mouse tailbuds.

claim: A general developmental slowing of explanted zebrafish tissue has been previously reported.
source: However, a general developmental slowing of explanted zebrafish tissue has been previously reported (Langenberg et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The zebrafish segmentation clock can maintain stable oscillatory output over a three-fold change in frequency due to temperature differences.
source: The zebrafish segmentation clock can maintain stable oscillatory output over a three-fold change in frequency due to temperature differences (Schröter et al., 2008), suggesting that its mechanism is robust to alterations in global growth conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The period inferred from the low-density data set was approximately two-fold longer than that of explanted tailbuds using the same time series analysis.
source: The period inferred from the low-density data set was approximately two-fold longer than that of explanted tailbuds using the same time series analysis (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental measurements from low-density cells and explanted tailbuds.

claim: Coupling with time delays between segmentation clock cells in the zebrafish leads to a decrease in the period of the synchronized population.
source: This supports the expectation that coupling with time delays between segmentation clock cells in the zebrafish leads to a decrease in the period of the synchronized population (Herrgen et al., 2010; Morelli et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The magnitude of the difference in period is larger than anticipated from the segmentation period of intact embryos with reduced Delta-Notch signaling, where the effect of delayed coupling was estimated at 20%.
source: However, the magnitude of the difference is larger than anticipated from the segmentation period of intact embryos with reduced Delta-Notch signaling, where the effect of delayed coupling was estimated at 20% (Herrgen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental findings to previous estimates.

claim: Fgf8b does not affect period.
source: Our own observations with a range of Fgf8b concentrations indicate that it does not affect period (Figure 1—figure supplement 8D, and data not shown), suggesting that Fgf signaling is unlikely to be responsible.
evidence: This is a finding from experimental data.

claim: Fgf appears to be permissive for the oscillatory state rather than instructive for the period of oscillations.
source: In this assay, rather than being instructive for the period of oscillations (Ishimatsu et al., 2010), Fgf appears to be permissive for the oscillatory state (Dubrulle et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Individual cells have a longer period than the period in the tissue.
source: In summary, our results demonstrate that individual cells have a longer period than the period in the tissue.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The results provide independent support for a role for collective processes in determining the period of the tissue-level segmentation clock.
source: Thus, they provide independent support for a role for collective processes in determining the period of the tissue-level segmentation clock.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The heterogeneity of oscillations across the population of cells can be described as the trajectories of self-sustained oscillators in the vicinity of a Hopf bifurcation.
source: We propose that this heterogeneity can be described as the trajectories of self-sustained oscillators in the vicinity of a Hopf bifurcation.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Excursions across the bifurcation stop and start cycling behavior, but the underlying oscillatory mechanism remains.
source: In this scenario, excursions across the bifurcation stop and start cycling behavior, but the underlying oscillatory mechanism remains.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Fgf signalling appears to push the oscillators above the Hopf bifurcation.
source: Fgf signalling appears to push the oscillators above this bifurcation, and the characteristic longer-timescales in the amplitude noise that we have observed may come from the inherent dynamics of the Erk network downstream of the Fgf receptor (Aoki et al., 2013; Albeck et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the experimental data supported by citations.

claim: The characteristic longer-timescales in the amplitude noise may come from the inherent dynamics of the Erk network downstream of the Fgf receptor.
source: Fgf signalling appears to push the oscillators above this bifurcation, and the characteristic longer-timescales in the amplitude noise that we have observed may come from the inherent dynamics of the Erk network downstream of the Fgf receptor (Aoki et al., 2013; Albeck et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Oscillators in the vicinity of a bifurcation may be more readily synchronized by coupling.
source: One feature of oscillators in the vicinity of a bifurcation is that they may be more readily synchronized by coupling (Gonze et al., 2005; Barral et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Individual cells from the mouse segmentation clock are also noisy.
source: Individual cells from the mouse segmentation clock are also noisy, but the contribution of cell-cell signaling to maintenance of oscillations, either by contact or through diffusible factors, remains unclear (Masamizu et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the mouse intercellular signaling may be required for sustaining oscillations, as has been observed for Delta-Notch signaling in neural progenitors.
source: It is possible that in the mouse intercellular signaling may be required for sustaining oscillations, as has been observed for Delta-Notch signaling in neural progenitors (Imayoshi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Striking the optimal balance between autonomous and collectively-maintained oscillations could be a tune-able evolutionary strategy in developing multi-cellular systems.
source: Striking the optimal balance between autonomous and collectively-maintained oscillations could be a tune-able evolutionary strategy in developing multi-cellular systems.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary strategies.
